# Results — Study 945 (The Hidden Financing) on the real daily tape

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). Regress each leveraged
wrapper's daily **total return** on **SPY**'s daily total return; the slope is the
realised leverage, the intercept is the whole daily drag. Annualise the intercept, add
back SPY's own fee so the drag is on an **index** basis, strip the fund's published
expense ratio, divide by the ``L − 1`` dollars actually borrowed — what is left is the
**implied financing rate**. Compare with **^IRX** (the 13-week T-bill discount rate, a
quoted rate in percent, *not* a total-return series). Common SSO ∩ UPRO ∩ SPY ∩ BIL ∩
^IRX ∩ ^GSPC window 2009-06-26 → 2026-06-30. As-of **2026-06-30** (the partial current
month is dropped) — data stamp as-of 2026-06-30.*

## Data stamp

| Legs | Window | n days | Fingerprint |
|---|---|---|---|
| SSO (2x), UPRO (3x), SPY (bench), BIL (cash), ^IRX (rate), ^GSPC (price index) | 2009-06-26 → 2026-06-30 | 4,276 | Fingerprint `1c447f91bfae` |

Mean ^IRX over the window **1.396%**; BIL's realised total return **1.267%/yr** — the
0.129 pp gap is BIL's own expense ratio, a useful reminder that the *quoted* bill rate and
the *investable* cash leg are not the same object.

**^IRX is quoted on a bank-discount basis** (labelled PROXY). The bond-equivalent yield an
investor actually earns is a little higher — 1.396% discount ≈ **1.420% BEY** over this
window — so every "spread over ^IRX" below is overstated by roughly **2-3 bp**. Small
against a ~68 bp mark-up, and it cuts *against* this study's conclusion, so nothing is
rescued by ignoring it.

*The fingerprint is a byte hash of all six legs read from the **shared** `studies/_cache`,
which other studies refresh. A re-fetch can move the hash without moving a single reported
estimate; this run reproduces every number below to the printed digit.*

## The headline — what the wrappers actually charge for the loan

Free-slope OLS, Newey-West standard errors, drag expressed on an index basis
(SPY's 0.0945% fee added back). Expense ratios are the published prospectus numbers and
are a **labelled ASSUMPTION**, swept below.

| Fund | Realised beta (*t* vs *L*) | R² | Intercept, %/yr (*t*) | Drag, %/yr | Implied financing | Spread over ^IRX | **spread HAC *t*** |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **SSO** (2x) | 1.9972 (−0.27) | 0.99748 | −2.774 (se 0.208, *t* = −13.31) | 2.962 | **2.072%** | **+0.677 pp** (se 0.208) | **+3.25** |
| **UPRO** (3x) | 2.9894 (−0.63) | 0.99653 | −4.787 (se 0.375, *t* = −12.75) | 5.070 | **2.080%** | **+0.684 pp** (se 0.188) | **+3.65** |

**Which *t* carries the claim.** The intercept *t* of −13.31 / −12.75 tests only that the
drag is non-zero — which a 0.89% expense ratio guarantees before any interest is charged.
It is *not* evidence of a mark-up over bills and is not quoted as such anywhere in this
study. The claim is the **spread**, and its HAC *t* is **+3.25 / +3.65** — past the |*t*| ≥ 2
bar, and a factor of four weaker than the intercept *t* it would be tempting to quote.

The all-in charge — the one that does not lean on the assumed expense ratio at all — is
stronger still: **+1.567 pp** over ^IRX at 2x (*t* = **+7.52**) and **+1.139 pp** at 3x
(*t* = **+6.07**).

**What the residual actually contains.** Stripping the published fee leaves financing *plus
every other daily friction inside the wrapper*: swap spreads, counterparty fees, the
slippage of the daily reset, residual tracking loss. A return regression cannot separate
those from interest, so **"implied financing" is an upper bound on the pure borrowing
rate**, and it is written down as one. The all-in cost per borrowed dollar needs no such
caveat — a holder pays it whatever its internal name.

The two wrappers imply the same borrowing rate to within **0.8 bp**. That is a real check
on the estimator — nothing forces it — but it is **not two independent draws**: SSO and
UPRO are both ProShares funds sharing an issuer, a swap desk and a counterparty list.
Agreement rules out a mis-specified estimator; it does not independently confirm the level.
Neither realised beta is distinguishable from its stated leverage, so the intercept is a
level term and not a mis-specified slope.

**All-in cost per borrowed dollar** — the number a user actually pays, because the expense
ratio is levied on the *whole* NAV while the loan is only ``L − 1`` of it:

| Fund | Drag on NAV | Borrowed per $1 of NAV | All-in cost per borrowed dollar | over ^IRX |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| SSO (2x) | 2.962%/yr | $1.00 | **2.962%** | **+1.567 pp** |
| UPRO (3x) | 5.070%/yr | $2.00 | **2.535%** | **+1.139 pp** |

The 3x wrapper is the *cheaper* loan: the same fee is spread over twice the borrowing.

## Block-bootstrap CI on the spread (2,000 draws, 21-day blocks)

Resamples the slope-pinned daily drag series (``L·r_SPY − r_fund``) and pushes each draw
through the same arithmetic. The pinned point estimate sits ~4 bp above the free-slope one
— the size of the disagreement you would expect when beta is 0.003 away from *L*.

| Fund | Spread | 95% CI | share < 0 |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| SSO | +0.721 pp | [+0.390, +1.079] | 0.0% |
| UPRO | +0.768 pp | [+0.432, +1.114] | 0.0% |

## The trap: regressing on the price index

The S&P 500 as usually quoted (**^GSPC**) is a **price** index. Regress the funds on it and
the missing dividend yield, multiplied by *L*, swamps the drag and the answer inverts:

| Fund | Drag vs ^GSPC | Implied financing |
|---|--:|--:|
| SSO | **−0.888%/yr** | −1.778% |
| UPRO | **−0.694%/yr** | −0.802% |

A leveraged fund that borrowed at −1.8% would be a money machine. It does not; the
benchmark was wrong. **Total-return on both sides or the arithmetic is meaningless.**

## Rolling 252-day estimate through the rate cycle

Each window's estimate is stamped on that window's last day, so nothing at *t* uses data
after *t*. The companion ^IRX figure is the trailing mean over the identical window.

| Fund | Spread: mean | median | sd | min | max | pass-through slope (se) | intercept | corr |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| SSO | +0.545 | +0.546 | 0.437 | −1.928 | +3.791 | **1.058** (0.034) | +0.466 | 0.975 |
| UPRO | +0.603 | +0.604 | 0.405 | −1.308 | +3.148 | **1.061** (0.027) | +0.520 | 0.979 |

A slope of ~1.06 with a +0.5 pp intercept is the signature of a **pure pass-through with a
constant mark-up**: when the Fed moves, the wrapper's borrowing cost moves one-for-one and
the mark-up does not. (The overlapping windows make these residuals hugely autocorrelated;
the slope is descriptive, and the inference bar is carried by the full-sample regression.)

Selected years (SSO / UPRO implied financing, ^IRX, spread):

| Year | ^IRX | SSO financing | SSO spread | UPRO financing | UPRO spread |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|

| 2013 | 0.07% | 0.11% | +0.04 | 0.39% | +0.32 |

| 2019 | 2.15% | 3.09% | +0.93 | 2.96% | +0.81 |

## Robustness — two cuts

**Calendar era** (split 2018-01-01) and **rate regime** (^IRX below vs above 1%). The rate
regime is the cut that matters here: a 60 bp mark-up is most of the cost at the zero bound
and a garnish at 5%, so a spread that survives *both* rate worlds is a structural charge
rather than a zero-bound artefact.

The 2018-01-01 split is the sample **midpoint**, not a chosen date: it puts 2,142 days on
one side and 2,134 on the other. The *t* column is the spread's own HAC *t*, not the
intercept's.

| Fund | Cut | n | beta | Financing | ^IRX | Spread | **spread *t*** |
|---|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| SSO | 2009–2017 | 2,142 | 1.993 | 0.566% | 0.192% | +0.374 | **+1.74** ⚠ |
| SSO | 2018–2026 | 2,134 | 2.000 | 3.555% | 2.604% | **+0.951** | +3.33 |
| SSO | ^IRX < 1% | 2,587 | 2.010 | 0.797% | 0.139% | **+0.658** | +2.69 |
| SSO | ^IRX ≥ 1% | 1,689 | 1.973 | 3.955% | 3.320% | **+0.635** | +2.08 |
| UPRO | 2009–2017 | 2,142 | 2.981 | 0.572% | 0.192% | +0.380 | **+1.77** ⚠ |
| UPRO | 2018–2026 | 2,134 | 2.994 | 3.566% | 2.604% | **+0.962** | +3.89 |
| UPRO | ^IRX < 1% | 2,587 | 3.010 | 0.770% | 0.139% | **+0.631** | +2.83 |
| UPRO | ^IRX ≥ 1% | 1,689 | 2.951 | 4.032% | 3.320% | **+0.711** | +2.80 |

The sign is positive in all eight cells and the two **rate-regime** halves both clear
|*t*| = 2 (2.08-2.83) at near-identical levels — a 60 bp mark-up is most of the cost at the
zero bound and a garnish at 5%, so surviving both rate worlds says the charge is structural
rather than a zero-bound artefact.

⚠ **The calendar cut is where this result is weakest, and it is stated plainly.** The
pre-2018 half gives +0.374 / +0.380 at *t* = **+1.74 / +1.77** — *below* the bar, i.e. the
early sample on its own cannot reject "the wrappers borrowed at bills". The mark-up roughly
**doubles** after 2018 (+0.37 → +0.95, *t* = 3.3 / 3.9). Read honestly: what the tape
establishes robustly is the **post-2018** mark-up of about +0.95 pp; the full-sample +0.68
is an average across a period whose first half is a weak estimate of a smaller number.
Nothing here supports treating +0.68 as a forward constant.

## Assumption sweep — the expense ratio

The **drag is measured**; only its split between "fee" and "financing" depends on the
prospectus number. A 10 bp error in the assumed fee moves the implied financing rate by
10 bp/(*L* − 1), so the 3x estimate is twice as robust to it.

| Assumed ER | SSO financing (spread) | UPRO financing (spread) |
|---|--:|--:|
| 0.75% | 2.212% (+0.817) | 2.160% (+0.764) |
| 0.85% | 2.112% (+0.717) | 2.110% (+0.714) |
| **published** (0.89 / 0.91) | **2.072% (+0.677)** | **2.080% (+0.684)** |
| 0.95% | 2.012% (+0.617) | 2.060% (+0.664) |
| 1.05% | 1.912% (+0.517) | 2.010% (+0.614) |

Across the whole ±15 bp band the spread stays comfortably positive: **there is no
plausible expense ratio at which the wrappers borrow at T-bills.**

## The practical read — wrapper vs a self-financed margin account

The do-it-yourself arm holds *L* × SPY on margin at ^IRX + spread and resets to *L* every
close, exactly as the fund does. **One execution lag:** the position earning day *t*'s
return was set at the close of *t−1*, and the rate charged over day *t* is the one quoted
at the close of *t−1*. Turnover of the daily reset is *L*(*L*−1)|r| of NAV — 1.44%/day for
2x, 4.33%/day for 3x — charged one-way **against NAV**. Nothing is sold short, so no
borrow fee applies. Both arms are measured **excess-of-cash** (minus BIL's realised total
return). Margin spreads are **labelled ASSUMPTIONS** from public rate cards.

**Eligibility, not just price — the limit of the DIY arm.** Reg T caps a US retail margin
account's *initial* leverage at 2x, so the **3x replication is not available in an ordinary
margin account at all**; it needs portfolio margin, futures or a prime broker. Every UPRO
row below is therefore a *price* comparison, not an executable alternative for a retail
holder — as is the +0.75% prime-broker row at either leverage. No margin call is modelled
either: the wrapper's loss is capped at NAV and the margin account's is not. Both omissions
flatter the do-it-yourself arm, which makes the break-even a **conservative** line for the
wrapper.

**The *t* column is not evidence of an edge.** Both arms hold the same *L* × the same
benchmark, so the difference is a near-deterministic cost differential plus tracking noise;
its *t* grows mechanically with the assumed margin spread and with sample length. *t* = 39
means "the arithmetic is stable", not "39 sigma of alpha". The economically meaningful
outputs are the annualised gap and the break-even.

| Fund | Margin spread over ^IRX | Fund exSharpe | DIY exSharpe | Fund − DIY, %/yr | HAC *t* |
|---|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| SSO | +0.75 (prime-broker tier) | +0.792 | +0.811 | **−0.64** | −4.56 |
| SSO | +1.50 (low-cost retail) | +0.792 | +0.789 | +0.11 | +0.78 |
| SSO | +4.00 (mainstream broker) | +0.792 | +0.716 | **+2.61** | +18.59 |
| SSO | +6.00 (full-service retail) | +0.792 | +0.658 | **+4.61** | +32.84 |
| UPRO | +0.75 | +0.792 | +0.802 | −0.57 | −2.25 |
| UPRO | +1.50 | +0.792 | +0.772 | +0.93 | +3.66 |
| UPRO | +4.00 | +0.792 | +0.675 | **+5.93** | +23.36 |
| UPRO | +6.00 | +0.792 | +0.597 | **+9.93** | +39.12 |

Both funds land on an excess Sharpe of ~0.79 against SPY's **0.836** — leverage is close to
Sharpe-neutral before costs, and the ~0.045 they give up *is* the financing plus the fee.

**Break-even margin spread** (gross and net of the daily-reset friction). The reset is cheap
— 0.04%/yr for 2x, 0.11%/yr for 3x at 1 bp one-way — so cost barely moves the line:

| One-way cost | SSO break-even | UPRO break-even |
|---|--:|--:|
| 0.0 bp (gross) | ^IRX +1.427% | ^IRX +1.090% |
| 1.0 bp (net, headline) | ^IRX +1.390% | ^IRX +1.035% |
| 5.0 bp | ^IRX +1.245% | ^IRX +0.817% |

**The break-even is a full-sample, in-sample average, and it moves when you cut the
sample** — so it is quoted as a range, never as a constant:

| Cut (1 bp one-way) | SSO break-even | UPRO break-even |
|---|--:|--:|
| full sample | ^IRX +1.390% | ^IRX +1.035% |
| 2009–2017 | ^IRX +1.167% | ^IRX +0.811% |
| 2018–2026 | ^IRX +1.607% | ^IRX +1.255% |
| ^IRX < 1% | ^IRX +1.169% | ^IRX +0.827% |
| ^IRX ≥ 1% | ^IRX +1.748% | ^IRX +1.364% |

The *level* swings by ±0.3 pp across cuts. What does **not** move is the decision at
realistic retail rates: the break-even never rises above **^IRX + 1.75%** in any cut, while
mainstream retail margin sits at ^IRX + 4 to 6%. The conclusion is safe by a factor of
three; the precise break-even is not a number to quote to three decimals.

## Synthetic control (machinery proof only — never supports the stamp)

Synthetic wrappers built from a *known* financing rate, 24 years, a planted 0.15% → 5.00%
rate step, 5 bp/day tracking noise, 6 seeds:

| World | 2x recovered | 3x recovered | mean error | max abs error |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| planted +75 bp | +0.683 pp | +0.813 pp | −0.067 / +0.063 | 0.357 / 0.169 |
| null (0 bp) | −0.067 pp | +0.063 pp | −0.067 / +0.063 | 0.357 / 0.169 |

The estimator recovers the planted spread and stays centred on zero under the null; because
the two worlds share a seed, the *difference* of the two recovered spreads is exactly
0.750 pp with no residual noise. The detector is unbiased.

## Verdict

- **Signal — Real.** The charge is measured, not inferred. The statistic that carries the
  claim is the **spread's** HAC *t* — **+3.25** (SSO) and **+3.65** (UPRO) — not the
  intercept's −13.31, which only says the drag is non-zero and is guaranteed by the fee
  alone. On top of that: a bootstrap CI of [+0.39, +1.08] clear of zero, the sign positive
  in all eight robustness cells, both **rate-regime** halves clearing |*t*| = 2 at
  near-identical levels (+0.658 vs +0.635), the whole ±15 bp expense-ratio sweep positive,
  and the all-in charge — which needs no fee assumption at all — at **+1.57 / +1.14 pp**
  over ^IRX at *t* = **+7.52 / +6.07**. The rolling pass-through slope of **1.06** says the
  policy rate goes through one-for-one and the mark-up does not move.
  **Three things the badge does not cover.** (1) *Upper bound, not interest:* what survives
  the fee is financing **plus** swap spreads, reset slippage and residual tracking loss,
  none of them separable by a return regression. (2) *The early era is weak:* pre-2018 the
  spread is +0.37 at *t* = 1.74, below the bar; the robust finding is the **post-2018**
  mark-up of ~+0.95, and the full-sample +0.68 is an average, not a forward constant.
  (3) *Survivorship:* SSO and UPRO are the wrappers that lived, and both are ProShares
  funds sharing a swap desk — so their agreement is a consistency check, not independent
  confirmation, and the estimate is a **floor** for a cohort that lost members.
- **Tradability — Investable.** Not an alpha — a **cost decision**, and it survives the
  audit because the margin of safety is enormous rather than because the estimate is
  precise. The all-in charge is **^IRX + 1.57 pp** per borrowed dollar at 2x and
  **^IRX + 1.14 pp** at 3x; the break-even against a self-financed daily-reset replication
  is **^IRX + 1.39% / + 1.04%** full-sample and never exceeds **^IRX + 1.75%** in any era or
  rate-regime cut — against mainstream retail margin at ^IRX + 4 to 6%, i.e. safe by a
  factor of three, worth **+2.6 to +9.9 %/yr**. (Those races' *t* = 18 to 39 are mechanical:
  same exposure both sides, so the difference is a near-deterministic cost gap. They are not
  evidence of an edge and are not offered as such.) The honest statement of the rule:
  **if you are going to hold 2x S&P exposure anyway, the wrapper is the cheaper loan unless
  your broker lends under roughly bills + 1.2%** — a threshold no ordinary retail account
  reaches. Below it (prime-broker tier, ^IRX + 0.75%) the margin account wins by −0.64%/yr,
  but that tier — and the entire 3x DIY arm, which **Reg T does not permit in a retail
  margin account** — is not available to the holder the rule is written for.
- **What this study does *not* price.** Only the financing. The daily reset also changes the
  *shape* of the payoff (volatility drag, path dependence) — that is the subject of studies
  943 and 944, and none of it is netted here. Nor is any of this an argument for *using*
  leverage: these two wrappers took −60% and −77% drawdowns on this very tape.
